An ungulate is any mammal that walks on hooves.

Before diving deeper, it helps to understand what a hoof is, since the entire definition rests on it.

A hoof is a hard, thick casing made of keratin — the same protein that makes up your fingernails — that covers and protects the tips of an animal's toes. When you look at a horse's foot, that solid, solid block at the bottom is the hoof. The animal is essentially walking on its own modified toenails.

So ungulates are, in a sense, animals that walk on their tippy-toes, with those toes wrapped in a hard protective shell.

Not all ungulates have the same number of hoofed toes. Scientists divide them into two major groups based on this:

1. Odd-toed ungulates
These carry their body weight on an odd number of toes — usually one or three. The middle toe bears most of the load.

  • Horses walk on a single toe (the hoof you see is one giant modified toe).
  • Rhinoceroses have three toes.
  • Tapirs have three toes on the back feet and four on the front.

2. Even-toed ungulates
These carry their weight on an even number of toes — usually two or four. The weight is split evenly between the toes, which is why animals like deer and cows have that distinctive split-hoof look (called a cloven hoof).

  • Cows, sheep, goats, deer, giraffes, camels, pigs, and hippos all belong here.

The vast majority of ungulates are herbivores — they eat plants. Grasses, leaves, shrubs, bark, and fruits make up most of their diet.

Many of them are ruminants, which means they have a special multi-chambered stomach and digest food in a remarkable way: they swallow plant matter, partially digest it in the first stomach chamber, then bring it back up into their mouth as a soft mass called cud, chew it again thoroughly, and swallow it once more for further digestion. This allows them to extract maximum nutrition from tough, fibrous plants that most other animals can't digest efficiently. Cows, goats, sheep, deer, and giraffes are all ruminants.

Pigs and hippos are exceptions — they are more omnivorous and will eat a wider variety of food.

On every continent except Antarctica. They have adapted to nearly every habitat on Earth:

  • Horses and wildebeest on open grasslands and savannas
  • Moose and deer in forests
  • Ibex and mountain goats on steep rocky cliffs
  • Camels in hot deserts
  • Reindeer in Arctic tundra
  • Hippos in rivers and lakes

Here's something that surprises most people: whales, dolphins, and porpoises are technically ungulates according to modern biology.

This sounds absurd, but the evidence is solid. DNA analysis shows that whales are most closely related to hippos among all living animals, and that their ancestors were land-dwelling, even-toed hoofed mammals that gradually returned to the sea over millions of years. Their front limbs became flippers, their back limbs disappeared, and they lost their hooves — but their evolutionary origin is firmly within the ungulate family tree. Modern biologists group even-toed ungulates and whales together under the name Cetartiodactyla.

So technically, every time someone says "fish and ungulates," there's a subtle irony — some ungulates are the sea creatures.

Ungulates are among the most ecologically and economically important animals on Earth.

In the wild, large ungulates like wildebeest, zebras, and bison are the backbone of grassland ecosystems. Their grazing shapes the vegetation, their dung fertilizes the soil, and they serve as prey for lions, wolves, tigers, and other predators. Remove them, and entire ecosystems collapse.

For humans, domesticated ungulates — cattle, horses, donkeys, pigs, sheep, goats, camels, and water buffalo — have been central to civilization for thousands of years. They provided meat, milk, leather, wool, and labor (pulling plows and carts) long before machinery existed. Much of human agricultural history is essentially a history of ungulate domestication.
Quick mental image to lock it in

If you ever need to remember what an ungulate is, picture a horse standing in a field. Those hard, solid feet? Those are hooves. Any mammal with hooves = an ungulate. Horses, cows, deer, rhinos, pigs, giraffes, camels — they're all ungulates. And surprisingly, so are whales.
